lessons.title: Three well-known cases and what they prove
lessons.subtitle: COMPAS, Amazon's experiment and Gender Shades

sections.title: COMPAS: a dispute over two fairness measures
sections.content:
COMPAS is a risk-assessment instrument; its score was one input among several in decisions in parts of the US justice system.

In 2016 ProPublica compared more than 7,000 scores assigned in Broward County, Florida, with later arrests. It reported that Black defendants not arrested again in the observation period had been wrongly classified as high risk more often than comparable white defendants. (Source: Angwin et al., ProPublica, 2016)

Northpointe countered that within the risk bands the scores were similarly calibrated for both groups; Chouldechova showed that calibration and comparable error rates between groups generally cannot hold at once where base rates differ, unless prediction is perfect. (Source: Chouldechova, A. (2017). Fair prediction with disparate impact. Big Data, 5(2))

What is proven is a difference under ProPublica's error-rate measure; the analysis alone does not prove which data or design choice caused it. People have to decide before deployment which measure counts.

sections.title: Amazon: an abandoned experiment
sections.content:
In 2018 Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the project, on an internal experimental Amazon system for rating CVs. It was built on ten years of applications, many from men, and one model penalised terms such as "women's" and the names of two women's colleges. (Source: Dastin, J., Reuters, October 2018)

The team removed the identifiable gender signals but, per the report, could not guarantee the system would not fall back on other, indirect features. Amazon disbanded the project team by early 2017 and told Reuters recruiters had never used the tool to evaluate candidates.

The case shows a development risk: historical application data can carry earlier selection patterns, and whether a model takes them over also depends on target, features, validation and the deployment decision. The report does not establish a hiring decision caused by this tool. When you cite the case, give both.

sections.title: Gender Shades: error rates from 0.8 to 34.7 percent
sections.content:
In 2018 Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested how commercial systems from IBM, Microsoft and Face++ classified binary gender from facial images; the subject was gender classification, not identifying a person through facial recognition. (Source: Buolamwini, J. & Gebru, T. (2018). Gender Shades. Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, 81)

The highest reported error rate for lighter-skinned men was 0.8 percent; for darker-skinned women it reached 34.7 percent depending on the system. These are substantial intersectional performance differences in commercial products.

The authors also found representation skews in two widely used benchmarks. Without access to the training data, it does not follow that these benchmarks or one data distribution caused every vendor's errors. What holds is the measured difference under the study design; cause, transfer and today's product performance need separate checks.

quiz.questionText: Which finding did ProPublica report in the COMPAS analysis?

answerOptions.text: The system was technically defective and produced arbitrary results
White defendants were twice as likely as Black defendants to be wrongly rated high risk
Under ProPublica's measure, Black defendants without a later arrest were more often wrongly classified as high risk than comparable white defendants
The system was perfectly fair, but the dataset was too small

quiz.explanation: ProPublica measured different error rates; Northpointe pointed to similar calibration within the risk bands. With differing base rates, you generally cannot have both at once.

quiz.questionText: What is established about Amazon's experimental recruiting tool?

answerOptions.text: The model was deliberately programmed that way
Reuters reported gender-related ranking effects; Amazon said recruiters never used the tool on candidates
The system could not detect applicants' gender
Applications from women really were weaker

quiz.explanation: Reuters described an internal experiment that penalised terms such as "women's". That establishes a development risk, not a specific hiring decision.

quiz.questionText: What did Gender Shades find for commercial gender classification?

answerOptions.text: The systems recognised all faces with similar accuracy
Only cheaper systems had bias problems
At almost 12 percent, darker-skinned men had the highest error rate of the four groups
At most 0.8 percent error for lighter-skinned men, up to 34.7 percent for darker-skinned women depending on the system

quiz.explanation: The study measured substantial intersectional differences in binary gender classification, not in person identification. It proved no training-data cause per vendor.

lessons.title: Ethics on three levels: technology, company, society
lessons.subtitle: Who decides at which level

sections.title: Level 1: technology
sections.content:
Attribution methods such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) or LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) estimate, under chosen model, reference and perturbation assumptions, what single input features contribute to an output. They show no causal effect and do not automatically give a full explanation of the decision process.

A bias audit compares error or selection rates across sensibly bounded groups and needs suitable targets, denominators, samples and uncertainty figures.

For high-risk AI systems, Article 9 governs risk management, Article 10 data and data governance, including, where relevant, an examination of possible bias, and Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. Whether this already applies to a system depends on classification, role and the current application date.

Technical tests can make risks visible. They do not decide whether a purpose is lawful or socially defensible.

sections.title: Level 2: the company
sections.content:
Every deployment needs a named purpose, a responsible role, approval criteria and a documented escalation route.

Where the high-risk provisions apply, Article 12 requires a system capable of automatic logging. Under Article 26(6) deployers generally keep the automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, unless other Union or national law sets a different period. What information is then there depends on the system and the deployer's access.

An internal review body can help, but no rule mandates an "ethics board" across the board, and such a body needs expertise, decision authority, documented approval and an incident process. For reports of infringements of the AI Regulation and protection of reporting persons, Article 87 refers to Directive (EU) 2019/1937; scope and national law still need checking.

sections.title: Level 3: society
sections.content:
Society decides through laws, rights and routes of control what a system may be used for. The AI Regulation, data protection, equal treatment and fundamental rights can apply in parallel.

Article 22(1) GDPR concerns decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect a person. Paragraph 2 holds exceptions; for the cases under paragraph 2(a) and (c) (contract, explicit consent), paragraph 3 requires at least a chance to obtain human intervention, to express a point of view and to contest.

For relevant automated decision-making, Articles 13 to 15 hold information duties and access rights on the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences. They give no claim to source code or to an explanation of every algorithm.

quiz.questionText: Which retention duty can Article 26(6) place on deployers of high-risk AI systems?

answerOptions.text: Sending a monthly report to the EU AI Office
Generally keeping automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, subject to other law
Making every algorithm publicly accessible
Setting up an internal ethics board

quiz.explanation: Article 26(6) generally requires keeping the logs under the deployer's control for at least six months, unless other law sets a different period. The logging capability itself comes from Article 12.

quiz.questionText: Which statement about Article 22 GDPR is correct?

answerOptions.text: It creates a right to demand deletion of all your data
Article 22 bans every use of an algorithm in a decision
Article 22 gives a right to the source code behind any AI output
Article 22 concerns solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect; exceptions have to be checked

quiz.explanation: Paragraph 1 covers only solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect; paragraph 2 lists exceptions, paragraph 3 safeguards. No right to source code or deletion follows.

quiz.questionText: What separates the technical level of AI ethics from the societal one?

answerOptions.text: Societal measures are useless because technology moves faster than policy
Technical measures already fix what an AI system may be used for
The technical level has clear answers, the societal level has none
Technology can measure and reduce bias; society decides politically which purposes are allowed

quiz.explanation: A technically optimised facial recognition system can still be used for mass surveillance. Society decides through laws and rights whether that is allowed.

lessons.title: Three checks for real AI deployments
lessons.subtitle: Data, responsibility, oversight route

sections.title: Check 1: separate data from target
sections.content:
Historical data can hold earlier inequalities, measurement errors or selection decisions. Whether a model reproduces them also depends on sample, labels, features, target, optimisation, thresholds and deployment context.

Check:

- Where do the data come from, and who is represented in them?
- What counts as the right result?
- Which errors are measured for which groups?
- Was performance tested in the real deployment context?

COMPAS, Amazon and Gender Shades show three different problems that do not reduce to "bad training data".

sections.title: Check 2: map role to duty
sections.content:
The sentence "The AI decided" names no organisation and no legal basis. The AI Regulation assigns duties by actual role and conduct: Article 16 to providers, Article 22 to authorised representatives, Article 23 to importers, Article 24 to distributors and Article 26 to deployers. Article 25 governs when another operator counts as the provider.

This allocation says nothing blanket about liability or about who caused a specific discriminatory outcome. Data protection, equal treatment, employment or civil law can apply on top.

For the individual case, record:

- Who provides the system?
- Who sets purpose and deployment?
- Who makes or confirms the decision?
- Which provision attaches to exactly that conduct?

sections.title: Check 3: document it so others can retrace it
sections.content:
Document each step so another person can retrace it:

1. Document purpose, responsible role, data source and the human decision point.
2. For a significant automated decision, check whether it was solely automated, its effect, which exception might apply and which information or protection rights exist.
3. For suspected synthetic media, preserve the original source and check provenance and context as in Block 2.
4. Record finding, uncertainty and the next responsible route separately.

AlgorithmWatch (algorithmwatch.org), the Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org) founded by Joy Buolamwini, and netzpolitik.org publish independent investigations into algorithmic systems, bias and digital regulation.

quiz.questionText: Which statement describes the relation between training data and model effect precisely?

answerOptions.text: AI developers deliberately build discriminatory models
Models always use too little training data, whatever its composition
Developers unknowingly program their personal preferences into the model
Historical data can hold inequalities; the effect also depends on target, features, testing and deployment

quiz.explanation: Whether inequalities in historical data become a harmful effect also depends on labels, target, modelling, thresholds, evaluation and deployment.

quiz.questionText: To whom does the AI Regulation assign duties along the value chain?

answerOptions.text: Only the original AI developer
Nobody, because AI systems act on their own
Only the market surveillance authority of the relevant EU Member State
By actual role, e.g. providers (Art. 16) or deployers (Art. 26)

quiz.explanation: The duties attach to the actual role, and Article 25 can turn another operator into the provider. Check liability, data protection and equal treatment separately.

quiz.questionText: Which organisation founded by Joy Buolamwini researches algorithmic bias?

answerOptions.text: AlgorithmWatch
netzpolitik.org
Data & Society Research Institute
Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org)

quiz.explanation: Joy Buolamwini founded the Algorithmic Justice League (ajl.org). AlgorithmWatch (algorithmwatch.org) examines algorithmic decision systems in Europe.
